archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (goaltending-sunk)
archetype.definition: A Pittsburgh team that drives play like a playoff club at 5-on-5, but whose record is dragged down by below-league goaltending and the league's second-worst luck in close games.

report.headline: The shot share says playoff team; the save percentage and close games say otherwise.
report.take:
Pittsburgh is 6-10-2, seventh in the Metropolitan and 25th on the site, on pace for 64 standings points. Its play at 5-on-5 doesn't match that record. A 53% CF % ranks 6th in the league and a 52% xGF % ranks 13th, so this team has the puck more than its opponents and creates more of the dangerous chances. Offense isn't the problem either: 3.22 goals a game sits right at the league's 3.2 and ranks 15th. The gap opens at the other end, where the Penguins allow 3.61 a game, 28th in the league, while giving up a roughly average 27.2 shots.

The goaltending accounts for most of that. The two goalies together are stopping .876, against a league average of .891, and both are below it on their own: Arturs Silovs at .873 with -2.3 GSAx over 12 starts, Sergei Murashov at .880 and -1.5 over six. Pts vs Goal Diff at -3.9 (31st) shows the record is worse even than a -7 differential implies. The last ten games include one-goal losses to Utah (twice, once in overtime), Montreal and Vegas, plus only one overtime win. A 98 PDO and a 99 all-situations PDO (24th) describe a team getting the wrong end of the bounces, mostly in its own net, since its shooting % (.115) is essentially league average.

The numbers also hide some real flaws. The forwards grade a D despite name value at the top. Evgeni Malkin (16 points in 16 games), Tommy Novak (14) and Sidney Crosby (13) are producing, but Crosby sits 94th among centers on the site's tab and Ben Kindel is -8 with seven points in heavy minutes. Nick Robertson has seven goals and no assists. Defensively, opposing forwards are out-scoring their own averages against Pittsburgh (rank 28), and wingers especially (rank 29), so not every goal against belongs to the goalies. The B+ blueline, led by Erik Karlsson's 18 points, is the best group on the roster, though Karlsson's own 46.6% xGF % is the lowest among the regular defensemen while Kris Letang's is 56.1%.

History cuts both ways. Last season this core scored at a 3rd-ranked rate and reached 98 points while defending at a 24th-ranked level, and 2024-25 brought a -12.2 GSAx. Keeping the puck out has been a chronic weakness, not a new one. Still, a team with a top-six shot share rarely stays this far underwater. Better luck in one-goal games and league-average saves would push them toward a .500 points pace, but the hole and a 1-4 recent run make the playoff line a long climb.

strengths.title: Owning the puck at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Pittsburgh out-attempts opponents at a top-six rate and wins the expected-goals battle too. That reflects how the team plays rather than luck, and it matches the previous seasons' 51-52% shot shares, so it should hold. It's the main reason to expect the results to improve.

strengths.title: Blueline is the roster's best group
strengths.body: The defense grades B+ while forwards and goalies both sit at D. Karlsson drives the offense from the back with 18 points and seven on the power play, and Letang and Korczak post strong shot shares in their minutes. Opposing defensemen are held under their usual output (rank 11), so the rear guard isn't where goals are leaking.

strengths.title: Veteran center depth still scoring
strengths.body: Malkin, Novak and Crosby carry a forward group that scores at a league-average clip, with Malkin at 16 points in 16 games. Novak's 55.1% xGF % suggests his production is backed by real play. The scoring is spread enough that the attack isn't relying on one line.

concerns.title: Goaltending well below league average
concerns.body: The tandem's .876 save percentage ranks 28th, and neither goalie is above water in GSAx. Shots against are average, so the goals against come mostly from saves not being made. Some rebound is likely, but the team's GSAx history includes a -12.2 season, so a full correction isn't guaranteed.

concerns.title: Forwards allowing too much the other way
concerns.body: Opposing forwards beat their own scoring averages against Pittsburgh by more than almost anyone, with wingers ranked 29th. That points to defensive coverage problems up front, not just goaltending, and it fits a forward group graded D. Kindel's -8 in 17-plus minutes a night is the clearest example.

concerns.title: Recent slide deepening the hole
concerns.body: The last five games went 1-4 with 4.2 goals allowed a game, worse than the season rate. Combined with a -3.9 Pts vs Goal Diff, the record has fallen behind even the modest differential. That luck should even out, but the standings damage from these games is already done.

trend.note: A strong September opener gave way to a 4-9 October and a 1-3 start to November, with goals against climbing in the recent stretch even as the underlying shot share held up.

weekAhead.headline: A light two-game week: soft San Jose, then streaky Ottawa
weekAhead.body:
Only two games. First is a trip to San Jose, which sits 28th on the site with a -1.11 goal differential, a 43.2% xGF % and shots against at 29.8 a game. Pittsburgh should control this one territorially. The catch is San Jose's A- goaltending and 7.3 GSAx, 5th in the league, which is the main thing keeping the Sharks in games. Against that goalie, Pittsburgh's chance-creation has to turn into finishing.

Ottawa visits on the 14th at 11-6-1, but some of that rests on a 102.7 PDO and a +1.7 Pts vs Goal Diff. Its xGF % of 52.9% is solid, though its 49% CF % is below Pittsburgh's. Ottawa holds centers well under their averages (rank 6) but leaks to wingers (rank 26), and its power play converts just 13.2%, 31st. A split is the baseline; two wins depend on the Penguins' goalies merely being average.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against San Jose's goalies
keyMatchups.body: San Jose allows 29.8 shots a game, but its goaltending has been elite by GSAx. Pittsburgh shoots a league-average .115, so it may need more volume than usual to beat a hot netminder. This game will show whether the possession edge can turn into goals.

keyMatchups.title: Wingers against Ottawa's soft spot
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa lets wingers out-score their averages and gives them 45.8% of the points it allows, well above the league share. That suits Rakell and Robertson more than the centers, who face a tougher matchup against Ottawa's center-limiting structure. Robertson's seven goals on a 59.3% xGF % make him the one to watch.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams edge on Saturday
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa's power play is 31st and its penalty kill 22nd, while Pittsburgh's kill sits near league average. Both units are below the league here, but this matchup tilts toward the Penguins, so drawing penalties could decide a close game.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Silovs, or Murashov if he starts, can post an average save percentage for both games, since that alone would likely turn a 1-4 slide into a winning week.

restOfSeason.body:
The shot share is real and should keep producing chances, so the 64-point pace overstates how bad this team is. Expect the close-game luck behind that -3.9 Pts vs Goal Diff to even out, and the save percentage to drift up from .876 toward something closer to league norms. That would make Pittsburgh roughly a .500 points team the rest of the way. The limits are just as real: a D-graded forward group that lets opposing forwards run hot, and a recent history of bottom-ten defense. That points to a ceiling well short of contention.

The early hole matters too. Seventh in the division after 18 games, even a healthy finish probably lands somewhere in the 70s to low 80s in points, outside the playoff picture unless the goaltending flips from a liability into a strength. That would be the real swing.
swingFactors: Silovs' save percentage over the next month
Forwards tightening up defensively against wingers

confidence.note: Eighteen games is a small sample, but the shot share and goaltending signals are clear.
